deep.reconstruction:
Context: this is p. 20 of Riemann's printed paper 'Beiträge zur Theorie der durch die Gauss'sche Reihe F(α,β,γ,x) darstellbaren Functionen' (Abh. Ges. Wiss. Göttingen 7, 1857), Art. VII. The folio is an offprint page, not a manuscript draft; the only handwriting is a red-pencil margin note 'a_n = —'. Riemann is deriving the hypergeometric series and its Euler integral from his P-function. The integral representation is a characterization: P is multivalued with the prescribed exponents at 0, 1, ∞.

(1) Setup (previous page). Take γ=0, so the exponent condition α+α'+β+β'+γ+γ'=1 becomes α+α'+β+β'+γ'=1. Write θ = x d/dx = d/d log x. The P-function then satisfies
(1-x)θ²y − (α+α'+(β+β')x)θy + (αα' − ββ'x)y = 0.
[Mine] This factors as (θ−α)(θ−α')y = x(θ+β)(θ+β')y.

(2) Recursion. [Mine] Substitute y = Σ a_n x^n with n running over a coset of the integers. Using θx^n = n x^n:
(n−α)(n−α') a_n = (n−1+β)(n−1+β') a_{n−1}.
This is Riemann's formula a_{n+1}/a_n = (n+β)(n+β')/((n+1−α)(n+1−α')).

(3) Closed form of the coefficients. With Gauss's Π(s) = Γ(s+1), Riemann states that
a_n = C / [Π(n−α) Π(n−α') Π(−n−β) Π(−n−β')]
satisfies the recursion.
[Mine] Check: Π(n−α)/Π(n+1−α) = 1/(n+1−α), and Π(−n−β)/Π(−n−1−β) = −n−β. The two sign changes cancel, which gives the ratio above.

(4) The four local solutions. Because 1/Π has zeros at the negative integers, the series terminates automatically on one side:
- n = α+k (k ≥ 0) gives the solution at 0 with exponent α, i.e. P^α; likewise n = α'+k gives P^{α'}.
- n = −β−k gives the solution at ∞ in descending powers, P^β; likewise n = −β'−k gives P^{β'}.

(5) Gauss's notation. Gauss's F(a,b,c,x) has term ratio (n+a)(n+b)x/((n+1)(n+c)) and first term 1. Take α=0.
[Mine] By the reflection formula, 1/Γ(1−n−β) = (−1)^n Γ(n+β) sin(πβ)/π, and the two factors (−1)^n cancel. Hence a_n ∝ (β)_n (β')_n / (n! (1−α')_n), so
P^α(0, β, 0; α', β', γ'; x) = Const·F(β, β', 1−α', x).
Inverting with a=β, b=β', c=1−α', the exponent condition forces γ' = c−a−b. So
F(a,b,c,x) = P^α(0, a, 0; 1−c, b, c−a−b; x).

(6) Integral representation. Insert Euler's Γ-integral for the Π-factors in the general term and interchange summation and integration. This yields
x^α (1−x)^γ ∫ s^{−α'−β'−γ'} (1−s)^{−α'−β−γ} (1−xs)^{−α−β'−γ} ds,
taken between any two of 0, 1, 1/x, ∞. The sentence continues on p. 21: the integral is a P-function, and suitable endpoints and paths give each of P^α, …, P^{γ'}.
[Mine] Using the exponent sum, −α'−β'−γ' = α+β+γ−1. The integrand is therefore s^{b−1}(1−s)^{c−b−1}(1−xs)^{−a} with a = β'+α+γ, b = α+β+γ, c = 1+α−α'. Over [0,1] this is Euler's integral for B(b,c−b)·F(a,b,c,x). That matches the Art. VIII formula on the next page, x^α(1−x)^γ F(α+β+γ, α+β'+γ, 1+α−α', x).
errors: No mathematical errors found: the recursion, the Π-closed form, the reduction to Gauss's F and the exponent bookkeeping in the integral all check.

Minor imprecision: the step 'introduce Euler's integral of the second kind and interchange' is only sketched. In practice it amounts to the Beta-integral (Euler) representation, valid for Re c > Re b > 0. Riemann himself flags on p. 21 that path modifications are needed when the integrand is too singular at an endpoint.

results.what: Recursion a_{n+1}/a_n = (n+β)(n+β')/((n+1−α)(n+1−α')) for series solutions of the P-equation (γ=0) in θ = x d/dx form
results.modern_name: Frobenius / indicial method for the hypergeometric equation

results.what: Coefficients a_n = C/[Π(n−α)Π(n−α')Π(−n−β)Π(−n−β')], giving all four local solutions at 0 and ∞ in one formula (series terminating automatically via zeros of 1/Γ)
results.modern_name: Gamma-function form of hypergeometric coefficients; symmetric two-sided series
